title: Roles, Users, and Role Membership
subtopics: Separating administrators, applications, and reporting users
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Roles, Users, and Role Membership.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to roles and login capability.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Roles, Users, and Role Membership. Its primary job is to help you design least-privilege access, secure connections, prevent injection and test row-level security explicitly. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing roles, users, and role membership teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: design least-privilege access, secure connections, prevent injection and test row-level security explicitly. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Roles, Users, and Role Membership
content_blocks.code:
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE products TO app_reader;
REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLE products FROM app_reader;
content_blocks.expected_output: The app_reader role is granted read access and explicitly loses the listed write privileges, assuming the role and table exist.
content_blocks.safety_note: Do not grant application roles superuser or broad schema privileges just to make a demo pass.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Requires an authorized owner/admin in a disposable database; inspect effective privileges afterward.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Security checkpoint: database privileges and row-level security are separate controls. Test as the real restricted application role; owners and roles with BYPASSRLS may behave differently.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Roles, Users, and Role Membership”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Roles and login capability”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Roles and login capability”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Roles, Users, and Role Membership, with an explanation of “Roles and login capability”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Roles, Users, and Role Membership fits into the broader goal to design least-privilege access, secure connections, prevent injection and test row-level security explicitly.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Roles and login capability, Role membership, Inherited privileges.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
